messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Darnell was 34, an African American parole officer in a busy county office, and he came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed around a single relationship he could not quite outrun in his own mind. The abuse had occurred with a former romantic partner, a man who, over time, moved from jealous remarks to threats and physical assaults that Darnell still described in clipped, careful terms. What stayed with him most was not only the pain of the blows but the way ordinary moments had become loaded with danger: the sharp antiseptic smell of the emergency room when he finally went in after one assault, the humiliating feeling of being looked at sexually by other men when he was already on edge, and the particular dread he felt whenever he found himself alone with men who seemed bigger, angrier, or too interested in him. Even now, if he caught a hospital smell in a clinic hallway or in the break room at work, his body would tense before he had time to think, his shoulders rising and his stomach tightening, as if the danger were already in the room.

Those moments did more than startle him. They pulled him back into what he had lived through, and the memory came with a force that made it feel less like recollection than repetition. He would suddenly hear pieces of what had been said during the assaults, as if the words were hanging in the air around him again, and he could taste the metallic bitterness of the night he had tried to swallow fear and saliva at the same time. When that happened, the memory did not feel past; it landed in the present tense, and with it came the conviction that what had happened had ruined everything. Darnell had come to believe his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that it was deeply unfair that nothing had been done about it, and that there was no real future worth wanting. In those moments he found himself thinking that maybe life was not worth living anymore, not in a dramatic or impulsive way, but with the weary certainty of someone who felt he had already lost something essential.

From there, his body seemed to take over. He was constantly tense and ready to react, scanning every room, street corner, and office doorway for signs of danger, and watching people closely for the smallest cues that they might harm him. That alertness fed the memory, because the more he watched, the more his mind caught on gestures, voices, smells, or a man standing too close, and each cue could bring the scene rushing back. The memory in turn made his threat system flare harder, leaving him more convinced that his surroundings were unsafe and that other people could turn on him without warning. It also intensified his appraisals: if the past could still seize him like this, then, in his mind, the trauma had not ended and he had been fundamentally damaged by it.

Those beliefs shaped the ways he tried to cope. Darnell pushed away positive feelings because they felt unsafe, as if letting himself feel good would lower his guard and invite another collapse. He avoided eye contact with coworkers, clients, and strangers, especially men, because looking directly at someone felt too exposing and too likely to invite attention. He also avoided any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, which was a serious problem in his work as a parole officer, where tense conversations were routine. He began taking longer routes through the office, keeping doors between himself and others, and minimizing conversations that might become heated. He did this partly because he felt constantly on alert, and partly because the memory made any conflict feel like the start of the old violence again. Yet these strategies quietly fed the cycle: by avoiding eye contact and conflict, he became more inward and watchful, which made him notice threat everywhere; by trying to suppress any hopeful or warm feeling, he felt more cut off and alone, which made the trauma seem even more final. The more he withdrew, the more his surroundings seemed threatening.

That withdrawal also changed the very triggers that could reach him. At work, hospital odor from a nearby clinic attached to the parole office, or the cologne of a man standing too close in the elevator, or a client’s lingering stare, could all set off the same immediate tightening in his body. Because he had learned to stay guarded and avoid confrontation, he rarely challenged these moments or let himself settle into them; instead, he braced, scanned, and watched, which kept the danger feeling alive and made the memories more likely to surface. He noticed that each time he had one of those intrusive moments, he left the encounter more convinced that he was unsafe and more certain that his life had been altered beyond repair.

By the time he sought help, Darnell was still functioning at work, but only by living in constant restraint. He had come because the fear, the vigilance, and the hopelessness were becoming harder to hide from his partner and harder to manage during long days with clients. What frightened him most was that he did not trust himself to feel safe even in ordinary places, and what he hoped for, though he could barely say it at first, was the chance to stop living as if the abuse were still happening in the next room.
